title: 1 Kings 1:28–40
context: David answers by calling Bathsheba in. He vows, “As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,” that he will most certainly do today what he swore by the LORD, the God of Israel: “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place;” Bathsheba bows with her face to the earth and says, “Let my lord King David live forever!” David then calls Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and commands them to take the servants of their lord, cause Solomon to ride on the king’s own mule, and bring him down to Gihon. There Zadok and Nathan are to anoint him king over Israel, the trumpet is to be blown, and the people are to say, “Long live King Solomon!” Solomon is to come up and sit on David’s throne, king in his place, appointed prince over Israel and over Judah. Benaiah answers, “Amen.” and prays that the LORD will be with Solomon and make his throne greater than David’s. The command is carried out: Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites have Solomon ride the mule to Gihon. Zadok takes the horn of oil from the Tent and anoints him; they blow the trumpet, and all the people say, “Long live King Solomon!” The people come up after him, piping and rejoicing with great joy, “so that the earth shook with their sound.” Both traditions read the unit as David keeping the oath and seating Solomon in public, a shared concern for the kingdom, not a private bargain.

verses.text: Then King David answered, “Call Bathsheba in to me.” She came into the king’s presence and stood before the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then King David answered, “Call Bathsheba in to me.” She comes into his presence and stands before him. The wording suggests that she had withdrawn, at least from the immediate place of speech, when Nathan entered; the narrator does not pause to explain the movement, and it should not be over-specified.

Arminian readers hear David taking the hearing back into his own hands. He calls her, and he will speak the next word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the king opening his answer by summoning Bathsheba again. Whether she had stepped aside only a little or left the room, the text simply says that he called her in, and that she stood before him.

Both traditions take the summons as the start of David’s public resolve, not as a slight to Nathan.

verses.text: The king vowed and said, “As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,
verses.arminianNotes:
The king vowed and said, “As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,” beginning a vow that runs on into the next verse. David swears by the living LORD, and he names that LORD as the one who has redeemed his soul from every trouble.

Arminian readers hear a free and solemn oath. David binds himself in the LORD’s name, in gratitude for a life actually delivered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the vow is made “As the LORD lives,” and that David’s past redemption is the ground he names. The king does not speak a casual word about the throne.

Both traditions receive the opening of the vow as shared confession: the LORD lives, and he has redeemed David’s soul out of all adversity.

verses.text: most certainly as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, ‘Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place;’ I will most certainly do this today.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The vow is completed: “most certainly as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel,” saying, “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place;” and, “I will most certainly do this today.” David confirms the earlier oath and sets it in the present day.

Arminian readers hear him freely keep a word he had sworn. The throne in his place is assigned to Solomon now, not left to chance after his death.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear certainty twice over: as he swore, he will most certainly do this today. The oath to Bathsheba is no longer only remembered; it is enacted.

Both traditions take this confirmation as shared ground. David’s concern for the kingdom and for the vow he made is now spoken in his own voice.

verses.text: Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the earth and showed respect to the king, and said, “Let my lord King David live forever!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Bathsheba bowed with her face to the earth and showed respect to the king, and said, “Let my lord King David live forever!” The response is honor and a blessing on the king’s life, not a speech about her own safety.

Arminian readers hear genuine reverence. She has received the vow, and she answers with respect rather than with a demand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the bow and the blessing as the fitting reply to the king’s oath. “Let my lord King David live forever!” is her word in this moment.

Both traditions read the verse as court honor after a kept promise, without pressing the formula beyond a loyal blessing.

verses.text: King David said, “Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada.” They came before the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
David next says, “Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada.” They come before the king. The three who were not at Adonijah’s feast are now summoned together.

Arminian readers see David choosing witnesses and agents who can act in public. Priest, prophet, and captain are called because the next step must be done, not only spoken in the room.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same three names Nathan had listed among the uncalled. The king now gathers them for the anointing he is about to command.

Both traditions take the summons as the move from oath to public act, still on the shared ground of David’s appointment.

verses.text: The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.
verses.arminianNotes:
The command begins, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.” The speech continues through verse 35. Riding the king’s own mule is a public sign of royal appointment, and Gihon is the place David names.

Arminian readers take the mule and the journey as real acts David orders. Gihon is commonly associated with a spring near Jerusalem, but the verse itself only names the place; that identification should remain a common suggestion, not a settled claim.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the king’s own mule and the named site. Solomon is to be seen on David’s mount, going down to Gihon at David’s word.

Both traditions describe the charge as a public installation already under way in the king’s command, without turning the mule or the spring into a type.

verses.text: Let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel. Blow the trumpet, and say, ‘Long live King Solomon!’
verses.arminianNotes:
At Gihon, “Let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel. Blow the trumpet, and say, ‘Long live King Solomon!’” Priest and prophet are to anoint, the trumpet is to sound, and the cry is to be the same form of words already used for Adonijah, now given to Solomon.

Arminian readers hear a real anointing commanded, not a quiet family arrangement. Israel is to hear the trumpet and the shout.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the anointing is to be done “there,” at the place already named, and that the public cry is part of the command, not an afterthought.

Both traditions take Zadok, Nathan, the oil to come, and the shout “Long live King Solomon!” as the king’s appointed means of making the succession known.

verses.text: Then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne; for he shall be king in my place. I have appointed him to be prince over Israel and over Judah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The command ends, “Then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne; for he shall be king in my place. I have appointed him to be prince over Israel and over Judah.” David names his own act: he has appointed Solomon, and the throne in his place covers Israel and Judah together.

Arminian readers hear a definite appointment. Solomon’s rule is not a later accident; David sets him as prince over both parts of the kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise place the weight on “I have appointed him”. The coming up and the sitting on the throne are the public outworking of that appointment.

Both traditions read the close of the charge as David’s own settlement of the kingdom, shared ground for the acts that follow.

verses.text: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, and said, “Amen. May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah answers, “Amen. May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so.” He does not add a new plan; he consents, and he asks that the LORD himself say what David has said. The speech continues in the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a willing Amen and a prayer that God would confirm the king’s word. Benaiah’s consent is real, and so is his appeal to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the Amen is joined to a petition: “May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so.” The captain wants the king’s appointment echoed by God.

Both traditions take the verse as loyal confirmation, not as Benaiah seizing the throne for himself.

verses.text: As the LORD has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He continues, “As the LORD has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David.” The prayer asks for the same presence that has been with David, and even for a greater throne.

Arminian readers hear a real petition, not flattery only. Benaiah asks that the LORD be with Solomon as he has been with David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear blessing asked, not assumed. The greater throne is a request, “may he be with Solomon,” and it will be heard again when the servants bless David in verse 47.

Both traditions receive the prayer as loyal hope for Solomon under the same LORD who has been with David.

verses.text: So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David’s mule, and brought him to Gihon.
verses.arminianNotes:
The command is obeyed: Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, “and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David’s mule, and brought him to Gihon.” The Cherethites and Pelethites are often identified as David’s guard; the verse itself simply names them among those who go down.

Arminian readers take the procession as the public act David ordered. Solomon rides the king’s mule because they cause him to, and they bring him to the named place.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the list as given. Priest, prophet, captain, and these companies escort Solomon to Gihon on David’s mule.

Both traditions describe the descent as fulfillment of the charge, without pressing the identity of the Cherethites and Pelethites beyond a common description of them as royal troops.

verses.text: Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the Tent, and anointed Solomon. They blew the trumpet; and all the people said, “Long live King Solomon!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the Tent, and anointed Solomon. They blew the trumpet; and all the people said, “Long live King Solomon!” The oil comes from the Tent; Zadok anoints; the trumpet sounds; the people shout the words David had commanded.

Arminian readers hear the anointing actually performed. The Tent from which the horn is taken is not further identified here; it is commonly taken as the tent associated with the ark in David’s city, but that should remain a cautious reading.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the public signs: oil, trumpet, and the cry “Long live King Solomon!” The priest anoints, and the people answer as they were told.

Both traditions take the verse as the heart of the installation, the oath now made visible, without turning the Tent or the oil into a type.

verses.text: All the people came up after him, and the people piped with pipes, and rejoiced with great joy, so that the earth shook with their sound.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the people came up after him, and the people piped with pipes, and rejoiced with great joy, so that the earth shook with their sound.” The unit ends in a joy loud enough, the narrator says, to shake the earth.

Arminian readers hear a real popular gladness, not a staged whisper. The city will hear this sound in the next passage, and it is already described as great joy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise let the wording stand. The people come up after Solomon, pipes sound, and the earth shook with their sound.

Both traditions close the unit on that shared public joy. David has kept the oath, and Solomon has been anointed king in the hearing of the people.
